articles.title: ‘Reverse physics’ could help bridge the classical and quantum worlds
articles.summary: Physics is generally built on observations, then the maths that supports them comes later. Columnist Karmela Padavic-Callaghan takes a look at an effort to reverse this and rebuild the laws of physics from the maths up
articles.content:
Physics is generally built on observations, then the maths that supports them comes later. Columnist Karmela Padavic-Callaghan takes a look at an effort to reverse this and rebuild the laws of physics from the maths up

Can we reverse physics and get to a theory of everything? Panther Media Global / Alamy Stock Photo

There’s a bit of an open secret in physics. Even when our theories work well – and some have been rigorously tested for centuries – we don’t always fully understand them. We start with experimental evidence, then build mathematical models and theories, test and update them with more experiments and hope that it all adds up. Often, it does. But were a mathematician to ask what a theory we built this way is – that is, what type of well-defined mathematical objects comprise it – that isn’t a question that researchers can always fully answer.

“The sense from a lot of physicists is these are maths details and that is not really physics, so it’s not their job to set them straight,” says Gabriele Carcassi at the University of Michigan. But if we are to tackle the biggest problems in physics, such as marrying quantum mechanics with general relativity to produce a theory of quantum gravity, we may have to take a different tack.

That’s where the “reverse physics” programme comes in. It is Carcassi’s passion project: he spends his days trying to put physics on accurate, rigorous and meaningful mathematical foundations. He is mapping out the bridge you must be able to walk to fully connect mathematics and physics. Carcassi puts it like this: “When the maths is derived from the right physical assumptions, the physical assumptions can be derived from the maths.”

Advertisement

Like most physicists, I didn’t learn to think this way. All the concepts that were taught to me came from physics, such as fields or forces or even slices of space-time, then I’d learn just enough about what they are mathematically to know which equations predict their behaviour. If you asked me to define a mathematical object called a Lorentzian manifold, I am really not sure that I could, yet I have a fairly good mental image of the physical thing it is representing: space-time as the fabric of reality. Reverse-engineering a theory of a changing space-time, essentially the theory of general relativity, from ideas like Lorentzian manifolds and other mathematical ingredients certainly hadn’t been put on my radar throughout my education.

But Carcassi and his colleagues at the Assumptions of Physics project want to establish these equivalent, two-way definitions for nothing less than all of physics. It’s an enormous undertaking, to say the least.

Trained as an engineer, Carcassi fell into this line of work because he married a physicist, Christine Aidala at the University of Michigan, who had a lot of physics books lying around. Reading them puzzled him, particularly those on quantum mechanics. Whereas most people get hung up on the matter of which interpretation of quantum mechanics is correct – if and how a theory captures the objective physical reality of our world, or if there even is an objective reality – Carcassi found that every idea was missing something.

“To me, all these [theories, such as quantum mechanics] are models, and I need to understand when they’re applicable and when not, essentially what they’re supposed to describe and under what assumptions,” he says. While he was grappling with this, the situation got worse. “I realised that we don’t really understand classical mechanics,” he says. This isn’t to say that classical mechanics doesn’t work, but that some of its theoretical ingredients are ill-defined, in Carcassi’s view.

As we talked, I was reminded of my advanced mechanics courses where I learned about objects called the “action” and “Hamiltonian”. They are incredibly useful, and I can define them loosely in English, saying something about an object’s preferred path through space or about its energy, but I’d be offering intuition that I got through homework problems more than mathematical rigor.

Carcassi says his experience was similar. “You know how to use them. You know their properties, but what exactly are they describing? You don’t know. I basically started reverse engineering a lot of these things.” This is just one example of the kind of definitional work reverse physics could offer.

“The tagline is to find a minimal set of physical assumptions from which we can rigorously re-derive the laws,” he says. Ideally, this would resolve many existing physics paradoxes and puzzles, such as the role of measurements in quantum physics where objects seem to acquire a fixed reality only after being observed. If we understood the maths underpinning those scenarios better, we could ascertain whether the world is fundamentally fuzzy or if a solid reality exists after all.

In the past 11 years, the Assumptions of Physics team, primarily consisting of Carcassi and Aidala, has broken down essentially all of classical physics into a set of mathematical equivalencies that allow the researchers to run over that bridge between maths and physics in either direction. Notably, entropy – which quantifies whether a physical system must assume one very precisely ordered state, or can find itself in many more equally likely states – has emerged as a key player in their effort.

For instance, they have shown that restricting any change in the entropy of a system is equivalent to previously known rules for how such a system can evolve over time. Reverse physics has already illuminated connections between quantum and classical physics – according to the team’s list of mathematical concepts and assumptions that undergird all of physics, it seems that classical physics is akin to quantum physics, but with entropy made high.

Carcassi is currently working on a slew of quantum problems, and candidly notes that it will be difficult to tackle various features of quantum field theory (QFT), where quantum fields extend through all of space and infinitely large numbers are known to crop up. One of the central objects that physicists use for QFT computations – for instance, to predict outcomes of particle accelerator experiments – is the “path integral”, which even professors who teach it often admit is an poorly defined headache for mathematicians. I’ve personally been fascinated by this enough to have devoted to a chapter to the path integral in my book.

But Carcassi’s quantum hopes soar higher: he thinks reverse physics could help researchers marry quantum physics and Albert Einstein’s theory of gravity by providing sufficient clarity on how both can be built from a shared mathematical base. “How can we even proceed and try to get new theories of physics, if we don’t even understand exactly what we have in the current one,” says Carcassi. The quest for a theory of quantum gravity has been one of physics’ biggest and least fruitful efforts for decades, which makes any new approach welcome.

Intriguingly, the way reverse physics could interweave these two pillars is indifferent to many of the common quantum fights among physicists. Carcassi and his collaborators aren’t interested in whether the equations of quantum theory imply that we live in the multiverse or that, for example, everything in the cosmos is inextricably connected with everything else. They are interested in the commonalities between every possible mathematical framework for quantum physics, and whether any resultant theory that encompasses them all makes sense with how we can measure and observe the universe.

Trying to redo all of physics from the ground up in this manner isn’t for the faint of heart. But what intimidates Carcassi is mostly the lack of funding and broad interest into this type of nitty-gritty work in physics’ very foundations. With appropriate funding and a big enough team, the reverse physics programme could be completed within a decade, he says. It brings to mind a story from my college years.

Once, during office hours, I told a physics professor about all the maths courses I was taking in the hope that they’d make me a better physicist. “I just know there will be a moment when all the maths and physics come together, and I finally get it all,” I said. The professor chuckled. He said he’d been waiting for that moment for his whole career. I hope the wait will soon be over.
articles.reasoning: The article describes a significant and inspiring scientific effort to rigorously rebuild the foundations of physics from mathematical principles, aiming to resolve long-standing puzzles and unify quantum mechanics with general relativity. This has broad implications for fundamental science and could lead to breakthroughs benefiting society's understanding of the universe.
articles.personality_title: Scientists work to rebuild physics from math to solve big puzzles
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Physics usually starts with experiments, then builds math models to explain what happens. But sometimes, even after centuries, scientists don’t fully understand the math behind these models.

**What happened** – Gabriele Carcassi and his team at the University of Michigan are trying a new approach called “reverse physics.” Instead of starting with experiments, they want to start with clear math and use it to build physical laws. Over 11 years, they have worked on classical physics and are now applying this to quantum physics, hoping to connect it with Einstein’s theory of gravity.

**Impact** – This work is important because it aims to fix unclear parts of physics and explain mysteries like how quantum particles behave when measured. For example, they showed that the idea of entropy (how ordered or random a system is) plays a key role in connecting classical and quantum physics. If successful, their approach could help scientists finally combine quantum mechanics and gravity into one theory, something that has been very hard to do.

**What's next step** – The team plans to continue working on quantum problems and hopes to get enough support to finish their project in about ten years. Their goal is to build a strong, clear math foundation for all physics that could guide future discoveries.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Scientists are building physics from math up to better understand the universe and connect the biggest theories in science.

articles.title: Switchable Chlorine Atom Transfer Radical Reactions
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11348-zSwitchable Chlorine Atom Transfer Radical Reactions
articles.content: Atom transfer radical reactions—encompassing atom transfer radical addition (ATRA)1 and atom transfer radical polymerization (ATRP)2—provide a versatile route to synthesize functionalized small molecules and polymers. Using readily available unactivated alkyl chlorides3 instead of activated organohalides represents the state-of-the-art in this field, as this requires cleaving stronger C–Cl bonds in the substrates while preserving weaker ones in the products. Here we describe a dual-copper relay catalytic strategy to overcome this limitation. A dinuclear copper complex selectively activates the robust C–Cl bond of unactivated alkyl chlorides, while a mononuclear copper catalyst mediates controllable C–Cl bond reconstruction. The reaction pathway can be switched between ATRA and ATRP-type reactions in the presence or absence of the mononuclear copper partner, thus providing a switchable platform for chlorine atom transfer radical reactions. This protocol can not only enable synthesis of structurally diverse ATRA products and α-end-functionalized polyacrylates, but allow for direct modification of poly(vinyl chloride) (PVC) under mild reaction conditions. It demonstrates the successful utility of unactivated organochlorides in organic synthesis and polymer science.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant breakthrough in chemical synthesis and polymer science by developing a dual-copper catalytic strategy that enables switchable chlorine atom transfer radical reactions. This advancement allows the use of unactivated alkyl chlorides, which are more challenging substrates, expanding the toolkit for creating functionalized molecules and polymers. The method also enables direct modification of PVC under mild conditions, which could have broad industrial and environmental implications. The story is focused, detailed, and presents a meaningful innovation with potential wide-ranging benefits in materials science and manufacturing.

articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Chemists use special reactions called atom transfer radical reactions to build useful molecules and plastics. These reactions often work best with certain chemicals that are easier to break apart. But using tougher chemicals, like unactivated alkyl chlorides, has been difficult because their bonds are stronger.

**What happened** – Scientists developed a new method using two types of copper catalysts working together. One copper complex breaks the strong bonds in unactivated alkyl chlorides, while the other controls how the bonds form again. This setup lets the reaction switch between making small molecules and creating polymers, depending on which copper catalyst is present. They also showed this method can change poly(vinyl chloride), a common plastic, under gentle conditions.

**Impact** – This discovery allows chemists to use a wider range of starting materials, including tougher chlorides, to make new molecules and plastics more easily. Being able to switch the reaction type with the same system adds flexibility. Modifying PVC gently could lead to better recycling or new plastic materials without harsh chemicals.

**What's next step** – Researchers will likely explore how to use this copper catalyst system to make different useful materials and improve plastic recycling or manufacturing. They may also test other types of unactivated chlorides and expand the method to more chemical reactions.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A new dual-copper catalyst system enables flexible and efficient chemical reactions using tough chlorides, opening doors for advanced molecule and plastic production.

articles.title: Key oddity of quantum physics may run even deeper than anticipated
articles.summary: Quantum mechanics stands out by being probabilistic and a new analysis suggests that this property can be traced unexpectedly deep into the theory’s mathematical foundations
articles.content:
Quantum mechanics stands out by being probabilistic and a new analysis suggests that this property can be traced unexpectedly deep into the theory’s mathematical foundations

We are still searching for a non-probabilistic understanding of quantum mechanics Photo by H. Armstrong Roberts/ClassicStock/Getty Images

Quantum mechanics’ probabilistic nature has puzzled researchers for more than a century. A new analysis shows that ridding the theory of this odd characteristic may be even harder than anticipated.

Infamously, quantum objects can exist in combinations of seemingly mutually exclusive states, such as in the Schrödinger’s cat thought experiment, where the animal is in a mix of states that makes it seem both alive and dead, and also neither. Left undisturbed and isolated, the cat remains mixed, but if it is observed – if an experimenter opens its box, say – it abruptly reduces to just one, unmixed state.

How exactly this happens – a question known as the measurement problem – is among the biggest unresolved questions about quantum mechanics. At its heart is a mathematical rule named after the physicist Max Born. Researchers have long tried to derive the Born rule from mathematical ingredients that could eliminate some of quantum mechanics’ probabilistic oddness. However, Jiaxuan Zhang at the University of Oxford has now found that some of the most influential among these derivations don’t fully accomplish this task.

Advertisement

The Born rule is a recipe for converting information about a quantum object into probabilities that tell us the likelihood of observing particular outcomes. The rule is also a postulate, which means the founders of quantum mechanics assumed its truth rather than deriving it. But it is a troublesome truth because it means that quantum mechanics cannot offer information firmer than the probability of something happening, such as Schrödinger’s cat being alive 30 per cent of the time you open its box.

Zhang wanted to know if past efforts to derive the Born rule from mathematical assumptions, instead of simply postulating it, introduced any probabilistic ingredients at the starting point. If no such ingredients are needed, it might be possible to place quantum mechanics on more deterministic ground – and so make it more understandable.

“I think that if we can find the origin of the Born rule, maybe we can also find the origin of quantum probability,” says Zhang. She spent about two years combing through five of the most influential derivations of the rule in an attempt to zero in on that origin.

Subscriber-only newsletter Sign up to Lost in Space-Time Sign up to newsletter

These five derivations were motivated by a broad range of ideas about how to interpret the equations of quantum mechanics, drawing on arguments ranging from considerations about symmetry and quantum entanglement to decision theory for inhabitants of the quantum multiverse. Zhang assumed an interpretation-agnostic stance and paid attention solely to the maths.

But as she dug into the underlying assumptions, she found more probability. “For people who want to derive the probabilistic Born rule from only deterministic principles, my result for now doesn’t support that,” says Zhang.

For instance, she concluded that some version of a concept known as additivity is indispensable to all derivations of the Born rule in her analysis. Although it can be stated more generally and abstractly, additivity is simplest to understand when thinking about fair dice. Here, additivity means that the probabilities of rolling each number, from 1 to 6, always sum to 100 per cent.

“I find Zhang’s paper interesting because it addresses a fundamental question: where do quantum probabilities come from?” says Augusto Smerzi at the Shenzhen Technology University in China. He says that, by showing just how important additivity is, she brings clarity to a long-standing problem.

But Smerzi says that clearly identifying the assumptions underlying the Born rule shouldn’t be misunderstood as an explanation for why this rule in its postulated mathematical form describes our world so well. “Making assumptions explicit is essential, but understanding why nature obeys them is what gives a derivation its deeper physical meaning,” he says. “I would therefore not interpret Zhang’s conclusions as closing the door to a deeper explanation of quantum probabilities. Rather, they highlight the importance of continuing to search for such an explanation.”

Zhang says the work is nowhere near over because there are more derivations of the Born rule that she wants to analyse. She also doesn’t think that some mathematical surprise is fully out of the picture yet. While her work constricts the possibility, there is still a small chance that the Born rule could be put on deterministic foundations, she says.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific analysis that deepens understanding of the foundational probabilistic nature of quantum mechanics, a fundamental theory with broad implications for physics and technology. It highlights progress in clarifying assumptions behind a key quantum rule, which is meaningful for the scientific community and could influence future breakthroughs in quantum theory and applications. The story is focused, detailed, and addresses a profound question in science.
articles.personality_title: New study reveals deeper roots of quantum randomness in physics
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Quantum mechanics is a branch of physics that explains how tiny particles behave. Unlike everyday objects, these particles do not have certain outcomes but only probabilities of different results. This idea has puzzled scientists for over 100 years.

**What happened** – Jiaxuan Zhang, a researcher at the University of Oxford, studied some of the main mathematical explanations for why quantum mechanics uses probabilities. She carefully checked five popular attempts to explain the so-called Born rule, which turns quantum information into chances for different outcomes. Zhang found that these explanations still rely on some form of probability at the beginning, meaning they do not fully remove the randomness.

**Impact** – This discovery shows that the randomness in quantum mechanics might be even more deeply built into the theory’s math than scientists thought. Zhang’s work clarifies which assumptions are necessary, especially a rule similar to how probabilities add up like the chances of rolling each number on a fair die. This helps scientists better understand where quantum probabilities come from and why they are hard to explain in a simple, certain way.

**What's next step** – Zhang plans to study other mathematical explanations for the Born rule to see if any can avoid starting with probability. Although her findings make it harder to remove randomness from quantum mechanics, she leaves open the possibility that future discoveries might offer a new understanding.

**One-sentence takeaway** – New research shows that the randomness in quantum mechanics is deeply rooted in its mathematics, making it harder to find a fully certain explanation for quantum outcomes.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une nouvelle étude révèle les racines profondes du hasard quantique en physique
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La mécanique quantique est une branche de la physique qui explique le comportement des toutes petites particules. Contrairement aux objets que nous voyons tous les jours, ces particules ne donnent pas de résultats certains mais seulement des probabilités différentes. Cette idée intrigue les scientifiques depuis plus de 100 ans.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Jiaxuan Zhang, chercheuse à l’Université d’Oxford, a étudié certaines des principales explications mathématiques qui justifient pourquoi la mécanique quantique utilise des probabilités. Elle a examiné cinq tentatives populaires d’expliquer la règle de Born, qui transforme les informations quantiques en chances pour différents résultats. Zhang a découvert que ces explications reposent encore sur une forme de probabilité au départ, ce qui signifie qu’elles ne suppriment pas complètement le hasard.

**Impact** – Cette découverte montre que le hasard en mécanique quantique est peut-être encore plus profondément ancré dans les mathématiques de la théorie que ce que les scientifiques pensaient. Le travail de Zhang clarifie quelles hypothèses sont nécessaires, notamment une règle similaire à celle qui fait que les probabilités s’additionnent, comme les chances de chaque numéro sur un dé équilibré. Cela aide les scientifiques à mieux comprendre d’où viennent les probabilités quantiques et pourquoi il est difficile de les expliquer de manière simple et certaine.

**Prochaine étape** – Zhang prévoit d’étudier d’autres explications mathématiques de la règle de Born pour voir si certaines peuvent éviter de partir de la probabilité. Bien que ses résultats rendent plus difficile la suppression du hasard en mécanique quantique, elle laisse ouverte la possibilité que de futures découvertes offrent une nouvelle compréhension.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Une nouvelle recherche montre que le hasard en mécanique quantique est profondément ancré dans ses mathématiques, rendant plus difficile de trouver une explication totalement certaine aux résultats quantiques.
articles.personality_title_es: Nuevo estudio revela raíces más profundas del azar cuántico en la física
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La mecánica cuántica es una rama de la física que explica cómo se comportan las partículas muy pequeñas. A diferencia de los objetos cotidianos, estas partículas no tienen resultados seguros sino sólo probabilidades de diferentes resultados. Esta idea ha desconcertado a los científicos por más de 100 años.

**Qué pasó** – Jiaxuan Zhang, investigadora de la Universidad de Oxford, estudió algunas de las explicaciones matemáticas principales para entender por qué la mecánica cuántica usa probabilidades. Revisó cinco intentos populares de explicar la regla de Born, que convierte la información cuántica en probabilidades para distintos resultados. Zhang descubrió que estas explicaciones todavía dependen de alguna forma de probabilidad al principio, lo que significa que no eliminan completamente el azar.
